sections.title: Long-term causes: MAIN & MANIA
sections.intro: War grew out of tensions that had developed over decades. The assassination in Sarajevo triggered a crisis within that already unstable system.

blocks.title: The two memory tools
blocks.text: MAIN = Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism. MANIA puts Nationalism before Imperialism and adds Assassination. The first four are long-term causes; the final A is the immediate trigger. Industrialization is another useful I because it supplied the weapons, transport, and productive power needed for mass warfare.

blocks.title: Militarism
blocks.text: Militarism means glorifying military strength and keeping a large standing army ready for war. Leaders treated military preparedness as a guarantee of security, but rival states saw it as a threat. An arms race could therefore make each country feel less secure even while it armed itself more heavily.

blocks.title: Examples to know
blocks.text: A unified and industrializing Germany altered Europe’s balance of power. Germany and Britain competed in naval strength in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; Japan also rapidly developed its armed forces. The military-spending chart illustrates the broader increase in spending before 1914.

blocks.title: How to explain a cause
blocks.text: Go beyond naming it: explain the mechanism. For example, military competition increased fear, encouraged planning for quick mobilization, and made the use of force seem a normal way to solve disputes. Several causes reinforced one another rather than operating separately.

sections.takeaway: Long-term conditions explain why a crisis could spread; the immediate trigger explains why the crisis began when it did.

sections.title: Alliances & the balance of power
sections.intro: Alliances promised security, but they also connected the risks and rivalries of different countries.

blocks.title: Germany and France
blocks.text: German unification in 1871 and France’s loss of Alsace-Lorraine deepened hostility. Germany feared French revenge and sought allies; France sought partners that could counter German power.

blocks.title: The prewar blocs
blocks.text: The Triple Alliance consisted of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy. The Triple Entente linked France, Russia, and Great Britain. The Franco-Russian alliance developed in the early 1890s; Britain later settled disputes with France and Russia as German naval power became a greater concern.

blocks.title: Geography mattered
blocks.text: France lay west of Germany and Russia to its east. Their partnership made Germany fear a two-front war. Austria-Hungary linked Germany to Balkan disputes, while Russia’s support for Serbia connected those disputes to the Entente.

blocks.title: Wartime membership changed
blocks.text: The prewar Triple Alliance was not identical to the wartime Central Powers. Italy remained neutral in 1914 and joined the Allies in 1915. Germany and Austria-Hungary fought alongside the Ottoman Empire and, later, Bulgaria. Britain, France, and Russia formed the core Allied coalition, which expanded during the war.

blocks.title: Reading the cartoons
blocks.text: The threats between figures and the falling dominoes illustrate how a local conflict could pull in connected powers. This is an explanation of escalation, not proof that war declarations were automatic: leaders still made decisions about threats, mobilization, and intervention.

sections.takeaway: Know both the membership of the blocs and how their geography made a regional crisis dangerous.
sections.note: Chronology clarification: the Triple Alliance formed in 1882, before the Triple Entente was complete in 1907. Slide 11’s “in response” wording reverses that sequence.

sections.title: Nationalism & the Balkan powder keg
sections.intro: Nationalism could unite a people, encourage loyalty to a state, or challenge an empire that ruled many peoples.

blocks.title: What nationalism meant
blocks.text: The slides define a nation through a shared culture, language, and history. Nationalists often argued that such a community should govern itself. Pride in one’s nation could also foster rivalry and a belief that national interests outranked compromise.

blocks.title: Why multiethnic empires were vulnerable
blocks.text: The Ottoman, Russian, and Austro-Hungarian empires contained many linguistic and ethnic groups. Demands for independent national states threatened to divide these empires. Compare the ethnic and political maps: cultural communities did not fit neatly within state borders.

blocks.title: Locate the Balkans
blocks.text: The Balkan Peninsula is in southeastern Europe, between the Adriatic region and the Black Sea. Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and neighboring territories lay in a zone of overlapping Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and nationalist interests.

blocks.title: Serbia and Austria-Hungary
blocks.text: As the Ottoman Empire lost influence, Serbian nationalists sought to unite South Slavs, including those in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Austria-Hungary’s annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1908 angered Serbia and made Vienna fear nationalist movements among its own Slavic subjects.

blocks.title: Why a “powder keg”?
blocks.text: The region combined territorial disputes, nationalist movements, and great-power involvement. Russia supported Serbia, while Germany supported Austria-Hungary. The powder-keg image suggests that one spark could ignite much larger tensions.

sections.takeaway: Connect Serbian nationalism → Bosnia-Herzegovina → Austro-Hungarian fears → Russian and German involvement.

sections.title: Imperialism & industrialization
sections.intro: Overseas competition and industrial growth connected Europe’s rivalries to the wider world.

blocks.title: Imperialism
blocks.text: Imperialism is the extension of a state’s control or influence over other territories and peoples. Colonies offered resources, markets, strategic positions, and prestige. Rival claims could deepen hostility between powers even when they did not directly cause the 1914 crisis.

blocks.title: Latecomers to empire
blocks.text: Germany and Italy unified relatively late in the nineteenth century; Japan became a modern imperial power after rapid state-led modernization. They entered a colonial competition in which older empires, especially Britain and France, already held extensive territories.

blocks.title: Industrialization
blocks.text: Factories could mass-produce weapons, ammunition, ships, and equipment. Railways and modern transport supported large armies; industrial economies could sustain fighting for years. Production made war more destructive without guaranteeing a rapid victory.

blocks.title: Read the visual evidence
blocks.text: Maps of colonial possessions show unequal access to overseas territory. Cartoons dividing Africa or China portray imperial competition. Factory photographs show the material basis for the weapons and supplies used in war.

sections.takeaway: Imperialism explains rivalry over territory and influence; industrialization explains the scale and destructive capacity of the conflict.

sections.title: The assassination & escalation in 1914
sections.intro: The Sarajevo assassination turned Balkan tensions into a diplomatic and military crisis.

blocks.title: The immediate trigger
blocks.text: On June 28, 1914, Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Princip was a Bosnian Serb nationalist associated with Young Bosnia; the plot had support from figures linked to the Black Hand network.

blocks.title: From a regional crisis to war
blocks.text: Austria-Hungary moved against Serbia, supported by Germany. Russia backed Serbia and mobilized. German leaders treated Russian mobilization and the Franco-Russian partnership as threats. Mobilization meant preparing and moving forces for war, not simply announcing a political opinion.

blocks.title: Key declarations
blocks.text: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on July 28. Germany declared war on Russia on August 1 and France on August 3. Germany’s invasion of Belgium brought Britain into the war on August 4. The wider declaration chart shows further entries as the conflict expanded.

blocks.title: “Nicky” and “Willy”
blocks.text: The slides introduce Tsar Nicholas II of Russia and Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany and their telegram exchanges. Personal and dynastic connections did not overcome conflicting national interests, military preparations, and distrust.

blocks.title: The counterfactual question
blocks.text: The class prompt asks whether war would have happened without the assassination. A strong response distinguishes a trigger from underlying causes: the assassination explains this crisis, but militarism, alliances, nationalism, and imperial rivalries made a wider conflict possible. Avoid claiming that either a single person or an inevitable “domino effect” explains everything.

sections.takeaway: Explain the chain of choices linking Sarajevo to a European war, while keeping the long-term causes in view.

sections.title: Expectations, war plans & the two fronts
sections.intro: The promise of a short, heroic war collided with the realities of industrial combat.

blocks.title: “Over by Christmas”
blocks.text: Early enthusiasm, recruitment imagery, and national confidence encouraged expectations of a quick victory. The slides contrast this romantic picture with a long war of exhaustion and enormous casualties.

blocks.title: The Schlieffen Plan
blocks.text: Germany planned a rapid defeat of France by advancing through Belgium before concentrating against Russia. The purpose was to avoid a prolonged two-front war. The plan depended on speed and assumptions about how quickly opponents could respond.

blocks.title: Failure in the west
blocks.text: German forces approached Paris in early September 1914. Allied resistance at the First Battle of the Marne helped halt the advance. Germany did not defeat France quickly and had to fight in both east and west. Fortified lines developed into a Western Front stalemate.

blocks.title: The Western Front
blocks.text: The main Western Front ran through Belgium and northern/eastern France. Trenches, machine guns, artillery, poison gas, and later tanks shaped fighting. The Marne (1914), Verdun (1916), and the Somme (1916) are the key battles listed in the slides.

blocks.title: Verdun and the Somme
blocks.text: The slides use these 1916 battles to show attrition: immense losses for advances measured in a few miles. Their figures are classroom approximations; a casualty can mean a soldier killed, wounded, missing, or captured. Do not treat all casualties as deaths.

sections.takeaway: The failure of a quick victory created a long struggle to wear down the enemy’s soldiers, supplies, and will.

sections.title: Industrial weapons & trench defenses
sections.intro: The central tactical problem was how to cross exposed ground while defenders used modern firepower.

blocks.title: Machine guns and artillery
blocks.text: Machine guns delivered rapid fire that could stop waves of infantry. Artillery bombarded trenches and advancing troops from a distance. Shelling created craters and mud, often making attacks harder even when it damaged enemy positions.

blocks.title: Poison gas
blocks.text: Both sides used chemical weapons. Different gases could cause choking, burns, blindness, and death. Gas masks offered protection, but gas added fear and suffering without reliably ending the stalemate.

blocks.title: Tanks
blocks.text: Armored tracked vehicles were developed to cross difficult ground and obstacles while protecting their crews. Britain first used tanks in battle at the Somme in 1916. Early tanks did not immediately eliminate defensive advantages.

blocks.title: Submarines and aircraft
blocks.text: German U-boats attacked shipping with torpedoes, linking naval warfare to trade and civilian supplies. The trench diagram shows aircraft observing enemy troop concentrations; aerial reconnaissance could warn defenders of an attack.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a trench system
blocks.text: Front-line trenches faced the enemy; support and reserve trenches held troops farther back. Communication trenches allowed movement and supplies between lines. Dugouts offered shelter, though a direct shell hit could destroy less-protected positions.

blocks.title: No man’s land
blocks.text: The exposed area between opposing trench systems contained shell craters, mud, and barbed wire. Wire slowed attackers, leaving them vulnerable to machine-gun and artillery fire. Defensive systems made an infantry advance extremely costly.

sections.takeaway: Explain the interaction of weapons, obstacles, and terrain—not just the names of the weapons.

sections.title: Life and death in the trenches
sections.intro: Soldiers faced continuous physical danger and severe environmental, medical, and psychological strain.

blocks.title: Unsanitary conditions
blocks.text: Cold, wet trenches, dirty water, inadequate sanitation, and exposure increased illness and suffering. Effective antibiotic treatments were not available to WWI soldiers. The slide’s estimate that about 12% of British troops on the Western Front died illustrates the scale of danger, not the rate for every army or front.

blocks.title: Trench foot
blocks.text: Prolonged wet and cold conditions damaged feet. The testimony describes swelling, numbness, severe pain, and sometimes amputation. It was an environmental injury, not a wound caused directly by bullets or a disease transmitted by rats.

blocks.title: Rats, lice, and other creatures
blocks.text: Rats fed on corpses and entered dugouts. Lice infested clothing and bodies. Accounts of frogs, slugs, beetles, and flooded trenches emphasize how difficult basic hygiene and rest became.

blocks.title: What testimony reveals
blocks.text: The soldiers’ quotations show lived experience through concrete sensory details. They provide evidence of conditions and perceptions, but one account cannot establish exactly what every soldier experienced.

blocks.title: Propaganda versus reality
blocks.text: Recruiting photographs and patriotic messages presented service as duty, honor, and adventure. Images of trenches and bodies challenge that idealized image. The All Quiet on the Western Front clips are dramatic representations; They Shall Not Grow Old uses restored archival material. The PDF supplies stills and viewing prompts, not the complete films.

sections.takeaway: Use trench conditions to explain the gap between wartime recruitment imagery and soldiers’ experiences.

sections.title: The Eastern Front & total war
sections.intro: The war consumed whole societies, and the two major European fronts did not develop in the same way.

blocks.title: The Eastern Front
blocks.text: Fighting in central and eastern Europe generally involved greater movement over larger distances than the prolonged Western Front stalemate. Trenches existed in the east too; “more mobile” does not mean that eastern armies avoided defensive positions.

blocks.title: Russia leaves the war
blocks.text: Heavy Russian losses and wartime hardship contributed to unrest and the 1917 revolutions. The Bolshevik government signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with the Central Powers in 1918, withdrawing Russia from the war at the cost of major territorial concessions.

blocks.title: Total war
blocks.text: Governments mobilized civilian labor, industry, money, and food for military goals. The distinction between the battlefield and the home front weakened because an army’s ability to fight depended on the whole economy.

blocks.title: Economic controls
blocks.text: The slides list nationalizing industries, rationing consumer goods, restricting strikes, and selling war bonds. Nationalization brought industries under state ownership or control; rationing limited consumption; bonds were loans from purchasers to the government.

blocks.title: Public opinion
blocks.text: Censorship restricted information, while propaganda encouraged support and morale. Governments tried to sustain commitment despite shortages and casualties. These measures show how war expanded state involvement in daily life.

sections.takeaway: Total war links battlefield endurance to production, finance, civilian sacrifice, and control of information.

sections.title: Reading propaganda critically
sections.intro: Propaganda seeks to influence beliefs or behavior. Study what a message asks its audience to think, feel, and do.

blocks.title: Four elements from the slides
blocks.text: Labels are written words that identify or frame meaning. Symbols stand for a larger idea or group, such as Uncle Sam representing the United States. Exaggeration enlarges or distorts a feature to emphasize a point. The main message is the belief or action the creator wants the audience to adopt.

blocks.title: Direct appeals and belonging
blocks.text: “Britons … wants YOU” and “I Want You for U.S. Army” address the viewer personally. “Step into Your Place” presents enlistment as joining a shared national effort. The posters frame participation as a responsibility and a source of belonging.

blocks.title: Guilt, family, and gender
blocks.text: “Daddy, what did YOU do in the Great War?” imagines future judgment by one’s children. “Women of Britain Say—GO!” uses family expectations and gender roles to encourage men to enlist. Analyze these as persuasive choices, not neutral evidence of everyone’s views.

blocks.title: Fear and demonization
blocks.text: “Destroy This Mad Brute” portrays the enemy as a threatening, dehumanized creature. “Wake Up, America!” personifies a nation that must respond to danger. Such imagery simplifies a complex conflict and can make compromise appear dishonorable.

blocks.title: Money, food, and work
blocks.text: Victory or Liberty Bond posters recruit financial support. Other examples promote food conservation and agricultural work. These are home-front appeals, demonstrating that propaganda mobilized civilians as well as soldiers.

blocks.title: A repeatable analysis
blocks.text: Identify creator and audience when possible; describe the labels, symbols, and exaggeration; identify the emotion being used; state the requested action; then ask what the image omits. A poster is strong evidence of its persuasive strategy, but it does not by itself show whether the audience believed it.

sections.takeaway: Connect a specific visual detail to a specific persuasive purpose.

sections.title: Why this was a world war
sections.intro: European rivalries drew on global empires, international trade, and military participation far beyond Europe.

blocks.title: Global participation
blocks.text: Britain and France relied on soldiers, labor, and resources from their empires. The slides’ British Empire casualty category includes Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, and South Africa. People from colonies were affected even when they had little say in the decision to fight.

blocks.title: Multiple theaters
blocks.text: The Ottoman Empire’s participation extended war into the Middle East; colonial possessions and sea routes connected Africa and Asia to the struggle. Japan and later the United States joined the Allied side. Fighting in Europe was one major part of a broader conflict.

blocks.title: Global economies
blocks.text: Naval warfare disrupted shipping, trade, food supplies, and access to raw materials. Factory output, overseas labor, and financial relationships connected civilian communities to distant battles.

blocks.title: Reading maps and media
blocks.text: Use the imperial world map and European battle map together: a conflict centered in Europe could mobilize resources worldwide. Film and documentary prompts add perspectives on experience but should be distinguished from the original written evidence and maps.

sections.takeaway: Give examples from participation, geography, and economics when explaining the word “world.”

sections.title: U.S. neutrality & entry in 1917
sections.intro: Formal neutrality became harder to sustain as economic ties and attacks on shipping brought the war closer to Americans.

blocks.title: The Zimmermann Telegram
blocks.text: In January 1917, Germany proposed an alliance with Mexico if Germany and the United States went to war. It offered support for Mexico to recover Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. Britain intercepted and decoded the message and shared it with the United States.

blocks.title: Read the original carefully
blocks.text: The decoded message describes unrestricted submarine warfare and a proposed Mexican alliance in the event that U.S. neutrality failed. It was a proposal, not proof that Mexico accepted or attacked the United States. The telegram also suggested approaching Japan to join the arrangement.

blocks.title: Unrestricted submarine warfare
blocks.text: Germany attacked ships in designated war zones without the usual warning and search procedures. This threatened neutral and civilian shipping as well as Allied supply lines. Germany hoped to weaken Britain’s war effort, but the policy increased the risk of American intervention.

blocks.title: The Lusitania
blocks.text: The slides show 1915 recruiting propaganda responding to the sinking of the British passenger liner Lusitania. Its sinking fueled anger, including over American deaths. It did not immediately bring the United States into the war; U.S. entry followed in 1917.

blocks.title: Was neutrality complete?
blocks.text: The export chart shows U.S. trade shifting strongly toward Britain and France while trade with Germany fell sharply. Political neutrality therefore coexisted with increasingly uneven economic ties. The chart supports an argument about economic alignment; it does not by itself prove the United States had already entered the war.

blocks.title: The declaration
blocks.text: On April 6, 1917, Congress declared war on Germany. The telegram, renewed unrestricted submarine warfare, and broader ties to the Allies help explain the decision. U.S. participation added manpower and resources to the Allied effort.

sections.takeaway: Distinguish political neutrality, economic relationships, and the immediate pressures that led to the declaration of war.

sections.title: Armistice & the human cost
sections.intro: The fighting ended before a final peace settlement was agreed, leaving immense losses and difficult questions about recovery.

blocks.title: November 11, 1918
blocks.text: The armistice took effect at 11 a.m. on November 11. It was a ceasefire, not the Treaty of Versailles. The agreement was signed earlier that morning; the slide’s 11 a.m. reference is the time the fighting was to stop.

blocks.title: Why Germany sought an armistice
blocks.text: Military defeats, depleted resources, worsening living conditions, and internal unrest weakened Germany’s ability to continue. These causes reinforced one another; the end of the war was not explained by one battle or one diplomatic document alone.

blocks.title: Physical and economic destruction
blocks.text: The slides cite about 22 million deaths and an economic cost of $338 billion. Treat these as the lesson’s estimates: totals vary by definition and methodology. Farms, cities, infrastructure, and economies suffered lasting damage.

blocks.title: Visible and invisible injuries
blocks.text: Soldiers returned with wounds, amputations, facial injuries, and psychological trauma. “Shell shock” was the period term for a range of wartime psychological and neurological symptoms; it overlaps with, but is not identical to, the modern diagnosis of PTSD. Societies struggled to support survivors. The slide’s example of Anna Coleman Ladd illustrates efforts to make facial prostheses.

blocks.title: Reading the statistics slide
blocks.text: The chart gives approximately 42 million Allied troops mobilized and 23 million Central Powers troops. Among the listed Allies, Russia has the largest death total. Germany, Russia, France, and Austria-Hungary together account for roughly three-quarters of the chart’s deaths. Keep mobilized troops, deaths, and total casualties separate.

sections.takeaway: An armistice stops fighting; it does not settle borders, reparations, responsibility, or long-term recovery.

sections.title: The peace settlement in the slides
sections.intro: The final lesson asks whether the settlement could reconcile security, punishment, national claims, and international cooperation.

blocks.title: The Paris Peace Conference
blocks.text: The slides date the conference to 1919–1920. The Big Four were Woodrow Wilson (United States), David Lloyd George (Britain), Georges Clemenceau (France), and Vittorio Orlando (Italy). Germany did not take part in drafting the terms on an equal basis, and Soviet Russia was excluded. Many colonial peoples lacked effective representation.

blocks.title: Wilson’s approach
blocks.text: The Fourteen Points emphasized principles including self-determination and international cooperation. The League of Nations was intended to help states resolve disputes and preserve peace collectively. These aims clashed with demands for punishment, territorial rewards, and the protection of empires.

blocks.title: The Treaty of Versailles
blocks.text: The treaty with Germany was signed on June 28, 1919. Its settlement included reparations, military restrictions, territorial losses, and the war-responsibility provision commonly called the war-guilt clause. The closing slides connect reparations and dissatisfaction with the question of whether the settlement could produce a durable peace. The wider Paris settlement involved additional treaties with other defeated powers.

blocks.title: A changed European map
blocks.text: Compare the before-and-after maps: Austria-Hungary disappeared, Poland reemerged, and states such as Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia took shape. New or enlarged states still contained minorities; redrawing borders did not perfectly match ethnic boundaries or eliminate nationalist disputes.

blocks.title: Mandates and unequal self-determination
blocks.text: Former German and Ottoman territories were placed under League-authorized administration by victorious powers. The Middle East map shows British control associated with Palestine, Transjordan, and Iraq, and French control associated with Syria and Lebanon. Independence was applied unevenly, especially outside Europe, helping preserve imperial influence.

blocks.title: Ratification and the U.S.
blocks.text: Wilson signed the treaty, but the U.S. Senate did not give the consent necessary for ratification. Opposition included concern over League obligations, U.S. freedom of action, and Congress’s war powers. The United States never joined the League and made separate peace treaties in 1921.

blocks.title: “A peace built on quicksand”
blocks.text: Germany resented the terms; Italy felt its gains fell short; Japan’s racial-equality proposal was rejected; China opposed the transfer of German rights in Shandong to Japan in 1919 (restored to Chinese sovereignty through the 1922 settlement). Colonial and Arab expectations of self-rule were frustrated. U.S. absence weakened the League. These tensions made the peace fragile without making another war inevitable.

blocks.title: How the closing classroom slides fit
blocks.text: Slides 122–127 contain simulation assignments and research directions. They are preserved in the Slides tab, including the class rosters and the final directions. They add no new core WWI concepts to memorize. Country-by-country motives from the opening handouts are summarized separately in the Paris Peace Conference tab.

sections.takeaway: The central tension: promises of a fair and cooperative peace versus competing demands for security, territory, compensation, and imperial power.

timeline: A new balance of power; France loses Alsace-Lorraine.
Franz Ferdinand is killed; the July Crisis follows.
Declarations and mobilizations turn the crisis into a European war.
The German advance is halted; quick victory fails.
Attrition and industrial killing for limited gains.
The United States enters on April 6; Russia’s political order collapses.
Brest-Litovsk in March; ceasefire on November 11.
Separate U.S. peace treaties; the Shandong issue is revisited.
